source.version: arXiv:2509.21685v2, 29 Sep 2025 (PDF p. 1); full text including Appendix 8 read.
source.title_on_document: FlexMind: Supporting Deeper Creative Thinking with LLMs

supplement.holds: Task descriptions, baseline annotation codebook, LLM prompts, additional participant ideation-tree visualizations, and expert-rating inter-rater reliability. The main idea-quality regression and its standard error appear in the main text (PDF p. 11, Table 2).

paper_design_summary: In a counterbalanced within-person study, 20 design and engineering professionals generated design solutions with FlexMind and ChatGPT, both using o4-mini; random assignment of condition order is not stated. Blinded domain experts scored submitted ideas on novelty, feasibility and value, combined into a geometric-mean idea-quality score. A separate single-condition study involved six senior practitioners using FlexMind on their own design problems, with qualitative analysis and self-reported experience ratings.

studies.label: Controlled user study: FlexMind versus ChatGPT

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each participant completed both design tasks, using FlexMind for one and ChatGPT for the other; task–condition order was counterbalanced. The mechanism used to allocate participants to orders is not stated.
assignment.quote: Each participant completed both tasks, one using FlexMind and one using the ChatGPT baseline, with task–condition order counterbalanced.

arms.name: FlexMind
arms.description: Structured visual workspace with schema-organized ideas, branching idea trees, tradeoff analysis, mitigation suggestions and contextual Q&A. The same participants also completed the ChatGPT condition (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1 and 4.1.3; p. 12, Figures 7–8).

arms.name: ChatGPT baseline
arms.description: Open-ended ChatGPT prompting using the same underlying o4-mini model. The same participants also completed the FlexMind condition; these are repeated observations of the same people (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1 and 4.1.3; p. 12, Figures 7–8).

participants.who: Design and engineering professionals with at least one year of relevant professional experience and a degree in their field, recruited through message-board channels at U.S. universities. Each person contributed to both tool conditions.
participants.quote: We recruited 20 design and engineering professionals (10 female, 10 male), each with at least one year of relevant professional experience and a degree in their field.
participants.locator: PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1.2–4.1.3 (recruitment and within-person design); p. 10, Section 5.1 and p. 12, Figures 7–8 (all 20 participants represented in results).

ai_tool.name_model: FlexMind and ChatGPT, both using o4-mini (also called GPT-o4-mini in Section 4.1).
ai_tool.how_used: FlexMind combines AI-generated seed ideas, tradeoff–mitigation suggestions, schema-based alternatives and free-text Q&A in a branching visual workspace; participants can add their own ideas and tradeoffs. The comparator is open-ended ChatGPT chat. Both conditions permit web fact checks, but ideation must use the assigned tool (PDF pp. 4–7, Sections 3 and 4.1.3).

task.description: Generate and develop solutions for cleaning laundry with less water and minimizing accidents from walking while texting; record ideas judged worth keeping in a structured spreadsheet for blinded expert evaluation (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.3).
task.duration: 30 minutes per task within a 90-minute remote Zoom session (PDF p. 7, Section 4.1.3).

outcomes.name: Overall idea quality (geometric mean of novelty, feasibility and value)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Four domain experts independently rated anonymized submitted ideas blind to condition, with two experts per task. The two raters’ scores on each dimension were averaged per idea (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4, Idea Quality Evaluation). Overall idea quality is the geometric mean of the averaged novelty, feasibility and value scores (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4). The main condition model uses a participant random intercept and reports coefficients in original rating-scale points (PDF p. 9, Section 4.1.6(1); p. 11, Table 2). An additional analysis of this same overall-quality outcome randomly sampled two submitted ideas per participant per condition to trace idea chain length. Its mixed-effects model includes condition, idea chain length, their interaction, and a participant random intercept (PDF pp. 9–10, Section 4.1.6(2); p. 13, Table 3). The random sampling concerns ideas and does not establish random assignment of participants or condition order. Figure 6 reports ChatGPT baseline n = 140 ideas and FlexMind n = 130 ideas. Its caption excludes 9 baseline ideas and 2 FlexMind ideas judged too vague to evaluate, plus 22 rubric-discussion ideas in total (11 per condition) (PDF p. 11, Figure 6 and caption). These are output counts and exclusions, not participant attrition; the same 20 participants completed both conditions (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1.2–4.1.3; p. 12, Figures 7–8). The figure-specific counts are not reconciled with the rubric-calibration passage, Table 1 or Appendix Table 11; n_units remains null pending clarification (see open_questions). Participants produced the ideas with the assigned AI tool during the task and recorded keepable ideas in a spreadsheet for subsequent expert evaluation (PDF p. 7, Section 4.1.3); timing refers to this immediate production.

contrasts.reported: Expert-rated idea quality: FlexMind M = 3.18, SD = 0.63; ChatGPT baseline M = 2.59, SD = 0.65; Welch’s t-test p < 0.001. Table 2 mixed-effects model, condition C(condition)[T.system]: Coef. = 0.473, Std.Err. = 0.115, z = 4.10, p < 0.0001, 95% CI [0.247, 0.699]. The model includes a participant random intercept; ratings are on a 1–5 scale. The coefficient is in original rating-scale points. Figure 6 gives figure-specific counts of 140 baseline ideas and 130 FlexMind ideas; see measure_detail and open_questions for the unreconciled analysis counts.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4 (expert ratings and geometric-mean construction); p. 9, Section 4.1.6(1) (model); p. 10, Section 5.1 (means, SDs and Welch test); p. 11, Figure 6 and caption (figure-specific idea counts and exclusions), Table 2 (coefficient, SE, z, p, CI and scale).

assignment.what_was_assigned: All experts used FlexMind on self-chosen design problems; there was no baseline or alternative tool condition.
assignment.quote: Experts did not use a baseline; the goal was ecological validity—how FlexMind supports real R&D framing, evaluation, and refinement when professionals bring their own tasks and constraints.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.2 and Section 4.2.1 (Procedure); single-condition study, so between/within-condition structure is not applicable.

arms.name: FlexMind
arms.description: Single tool condition for all six experts on their self-chosen domain-relevant design tasks; no baseline (PDF p. 10, Sections 4.2.1–4.2.3).

participants.who: Senior design/engineering practitioners recruited through professional networks, including a designer, a sensing/hardware research scientist, a robotics systems engineer, an industrial researcher and two senior PhD researchers with design backgrounds.
participants.quote: We also conducted a follow-up expert study in which six senior practitioners used FlexMind on domain-relevant tasks of their choosing, to complement the controlled comparison and gauge real-world applicability.
participants.locator: PDF p. 7, Section 4 (separate six-person expert study); p. 10, Sections 4.2.3–4.2.5 (participants and analysis); p. 22, Appendix 8.2.2, Table 9 (expert tasks).

ai_tool.name_model: FlexMind; the paper identifies o4-mini as the underlying model for the controlled comparison but does not separately specify the model for the expert sessions.
ai_tool.how_used: Experts used FlexMind after a tutorial and practice task, exploring their own design problems with the structured idea, tradeoff, mitigation and Q&A interface (PDF p. 10, Sections 4.2.1–4.2.2).

task.description: Each expert selected a domain-relevant, open-ended conceptual design problem not yet thoroughly explored and recorded keepable ideas; analysis concerned think-aloud/interview themes and self-reported experience, with no independently scored idea-quality outcome reported for this sample (PDF p. 10, Sections 4.2.1–4.2.5; p. 22, Table 9).

company_involvement.description: Coauthors Yan-Ying Chen and Matthew K. Hong are affiliated with Toyota Research Institute. This records company involvement through authorship; the affiliation does not establish a funding arrangement.

eligibility.reason: The controlled comparison has 20 analyzed people completing both conditions, below the codebook’s 50-person threshold (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1.2–4.1.3; p. 12, Figures 7–8). Counterbalanced task–condition order is stated, but random assignment of people or condition order is not, so criterion 1 remains unclear and design_class remains other (PDF p. 7, Section 4.1.3). Random selection of ideas for rubric calibration and chain-length analysis does not establish randomized condition assignment (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4; pp. 9–10, Section 4.1.6(2)). Blinded domain experts independently scored submitted ideas on novelty, feasibility and value, combined into overall quality, satisfying criterion 3 (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4; p. 11, Figure 6 and Table 2). Unreconciled idea counts concern outputs and do not change the participant count. The separate expert study has six people using FlexMind without a baseline and reports qualitative findings and self-reported experience, with no independently scored output outcome (PDF p. 10, Sections 4.2–4.2.5). Neither study qualifies for core inclusion; no codebook context class is established.

one_line_finding: In the 20-person counterbalanced comparison, FlexMind ideas received higher expert-rated quality than ChatGPT ideas (M = 3.18, SD = 0.63 versus M = 2.59, SD = 0.65; Welch’s p < 0.001; PDF p. 10, Section 5.1), with a mixed-effects condition coefficient of 0.473 (SE = 0.115, p < 0.0001; PDF p. 11, Table 2).
open_questions: How do the idea counts and rubric-calibration exclusions reconcile across analyses? Figure 6 reports baseline n = 140 ideas and FlexMind n = 130 ideas after excluding 9 vague baseline ideas, 2 vague FlexMind ideas, and 22 rubric-discussion ideas in total (11 per condition) (PDF p. 11, Figure 6 and caption). Section 4.1.4 instead says rubric calibration used 22 randomly selected ideas from each task (PDF p. 8); Section 4.1.6(1) confirms rubric-discussion and too-vague ideas were excluded before modeling (PDF p. 9). Table 1 reports High: 68 vs. 21, Low: 27 vs. 69, and Medium: 42 vs. 46 (FlexMind versus baseline; PDF p. 11, Table 1 caption). Appendix Table 11 reports Task 1 n = 112 and Task 2 n = 161 ideas for reliability (PDF p. 29, Section 8.5.2). The source does not establish one reconciled analysis sample, so n_units remains null. These counts refer to outputs, not people or participant attrition; the controlled study retains 20 analyzed people.
